passage:
(Arnab, 15, texting his friend Gopika on Sunday night)
Gopika: football trials tomorrow!! you coming? you'd be great 🙂
Arnab: nah
Gopika: why?? you're fast
Arnab: I'm top of the chess club. everyone knows me there
Arnab: if I go to football and I'm bad, the football guys will laugh and the chess guys will think I left them
Gopika: or you'd be good at both
Arnab: or I lose both
Gopika: you've been talking about football for a year though
Arnab: yeah. but right now at least I'm someone somewhere
Gopika: ok. but trials are only once a year 😕
Arnab: I know. staying home

qa.q: What is Arnab top of?
qa.a: Arnab is top of the chess club.

qa.q: What worries Arnab most about the football trials?
qa.a: He fears losing his place in the chess club and being laughed at in football, and that possible loss feels bigger than the chance of doing well.

qa.q: What could Gopika suggest to make the step feel smaller?
qa.a: Gopika could point out that trying football doesn't mean leaving chess, and offer to go along to the trials for support.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel reading "staying home"?
qa.a: Gopika may feel disappointed and a little helpless, after hearing him talk about football for a year and knowing trials come only once.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy skipping football trials because losing his chess-club standing feels worse than any possible gain.

passage: Every evening the boys of their village near Jorhat gathered at the tea shop to play carrom, and Bhupen, sixteen, was the champion. When Sabina told him the new youth theatre group in town needed boys for their Bihu play, his eyes lit up for a second. He loved acting; he could do every teacher's voice perfectly. Then the light faded. "The carrom lot will say I've become too good for them," he said. "And at the theatre I'll be the village boy who knows nothing." Sabina shook her head. "You'd still be you." "Here, I'm the champion," Bhupen said. "There, I'm nobody." That evening he went back to the carrom board and won three games. He didn't smile much.

qa.q: Which group needed boys for the Bihu play?
qa.a: The new youth theatre group in town needed boys for their Bihu play.

qa.q: Why did the light fade from Bhupen's eyes?
qa.a: He began imagining losing his place with the carrom group and being a nobody at the theatre, and that feared loss outweighed his love of acting.

qa.q: What small step could Bhupen take?
qa.a: He could go to one theatre rehearsal while still playing carrom in the evenings, testing the new group without giving up the old one.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Bhupen's choice?
qa.a: Sabina seems to believe he'd still be himself anywhere, so watching him choose safety over something he loves may make Sabina sad.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy turning down a theatre group he would love because losing his standing with the carrom group feels worse than the gain.

passage: In Cape Town, Thabo had been in the same tight group of four since primary school. They sat on the same bench every lunch and walked the same way home. This term, Lindiwe invited him to join the robotics club, where she and Beatriz were building a small rover. Thabo loved anything with motors. He went to the doorway once, watched them solder, and felt a pull in his chest. Then he thought of his friends. What if they felt he was ditching them? What if the robotics kids thought he was clueless? "Maybe next year," he told Lindiwe. At lunch he sat on the usual bench, half-listening, watching the robotics room window across the yard.

qa.q: What were Lindiwe and Beatriz building?
qa.a: They were building a small rover.

qa.q: What does Thabo's "maybe next year" reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: It reveals that fear of losing his place with his old friends and of looking clueless in the club outweighs the pull he feels toward robotics.

qa.q: What would you advise Thabo?
qa.a: He could tell his friends about the club and try a few sessions; joining robotics doesn't mean leaving the bench, and he would learn whether the fears come true.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Thabo says "maybe next year"?
qa.a: Lindiwe may feel disappointed, having invited him because he loves motors, and may wonder whether the invitation came across wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy avoiding a new club because losing his place in his old group feels worse than any possible gain.

subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
passage: At the city sports complex, Neel, fifteen, was the best badminton player in the under-16 group. Everyone at Court 2 knew it. When coach Kalyani ma'am announced a new squash programme, she looked at him. "You'd be good. Same footwork." Ritu, from his batch, signed up immediately. "Come on, Neel, it'll be fun." Neel shook his head. "I'm happy here." But he kept glancing at the glass squash court during breaks. He imagined walking in and losing to kids younger than him. Everyone watching the badminton star miss the ball. That picture made his stomach clench. At Court 2, he was number one. On the squash court, he'd be nobody. Two months later, Ritu was playing a friendly match on the squash court, laughing. Neel watched through the glass. He still won every badminton game. But the complex felt smaller somehow.

qa.q: Which group was Neel the best badminton player in?
qa.a: The under-16 group.

qa.q: Why did Neel refuse to try squash even though he kept glancing at the court?
qa.a: Losing his place as the badminton star felt worse than any fun or skill he might gain. The picture of missing the ball in front of others made his stomach clench.

qa.q: What small step could Neel take to try squash without risking his standing all at once?
qa.a: He could ask Kalyani ma'am for a private practice session or play with Ritu when the court is quiet, so he can be a beginner without an audience.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Neel's choice to stay only with badminton?
qa.a: Ritu might feel a bit disappointed at not sharing the new sport with Neel, and may wonder why someone so good is afraid to try.

grounding: A teenage boy refuses to try squash because losing his status as the best badminton player feels worse than any gain.

subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
passage:
Dear Anand,
Remember I told you about the new kids from the drama group who asked me to sit with them at lunch? I didn't go. I've been with the same four guys since Class 5. We're known as the cricket lot. I'm not even the best player, just the boy who keeps score, but I've got a spot. If I start hanging out with the drama people and it doesn't work out, I might lose my place with the cricket lot and end up with nobody. That scares me more than anything.
But here's the thing. The drama group is making a short film, and they asked me to help with the music. You know I've always wanted to try that. I said I was busy. I wasn't.
Sometimes I feel my world is the size of one lunch table.
What would you do?
Your cousin,
Tarun

qa.q: Since which class has Tarun been with the same four guys?
qa.a: Since Class 5.

qa.q: Why did Tarun say he was busy when the drama group asked him to help with the music?
qa.a: He fears that trying the new group might cost him his place with the cricket lot and leave him with nobody. That possible loss feels bigger than the chance to do music he has always wanted.

qa.q: What small choice could Tarun make to test his fear without giving anything up?
qa.a: He could help with the film's music for one afternoon while still sitting with the cricket lot at lunch, and see whether he really loses anything.

qa.q: If you were Anand reading this letter, what might you want to tell Tarun?
qa.a: You might want to reassure him that real friends won't drop him for trying music, and encourage him to say yes to the film.

grounding: A teenage boy writes to his cousin that fear of losing his place in his friend group keeps him from joining a drama group's film.
